According to the latest issue of Mark Gurman's "Power On" newsletter, Apple is reportedly considering changes to its App Store. The goal? To boost the potential revenue the platform brings in.

Apple's specific plans for the App Store remain unclear. Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman reports that Apple hopes to "find ways to improve profit margins and extract more recurring revenue from it," a direction being primarily driven by incoming CEO John Ternus and current services SVP Eddy Cue.

Reportedly, this work was one of the reasons long-time Apple executive Phil Schiller left the company last week. Schiller stepped down from his role as SVP of Marketing in 2020 to become an Apple Fellow, with part of his remit including overseeing the App Store. Schiller did not agree with the idea:

Apple has many ways it could improve App Store profit margins. It could eliminate the manual app review process—a costly procedure that's already less effective in the age of agentic coding. However, users might not appreciate further automation of app review, even if it would help reduce costs.

Apple could raise developer membership fees, currently $99 per year. Given that many small developers are already paying $200 per month for subscriptions to Codex and Claude to build apps, some might argue Apple has room to raise prices and developers would still pay. Apple could also charge large developers monthly fees based on traffic, passing on some of its infrastructure costs to them.

What the end result will be remains to be seen, but I'm personally excited to see what these changes end up looking like.
